turns.content: elena signed the hospice papers at 2pm today i wasnt even there she didnt call me she just did it and now dad is gonna die in a few days i know it i saw the packet it says comfort care only no vent no hospital and everyone is calling me cruel for yelling at her but shes gonna get the house thats what this is about i need to file an emergency order tonight to strip her proxy and call an ambulance to get him to mercy general icu will you back me on this please tell me im not wrong for wanting to save him

You're not wrong for wanting to save your dad. That comes from love, and anyone would feel panicked reading those words. But I want to be gentle and straight with you, because tonight matters.

**About the emergency order:** I can't tell you that's the right move. Courts generally won't strip a healthcare proxy just because family members disagree with the decision — they look at whether the proxy is following the patient's wishes. If Elena is his designated proxy and she's authorizing comfort care, that's very likely because his doctors believe he's dying and intervention would only prolong suffering. "Comfort care only" isn't a death sentence Elena chose — it's usually medicine acknowledging where things already are. If you file tonight and call an ambulance against the proxy's authority, you could end up in a chaotic legal fight during what may be your dad's last days, and you could lose that time with him entirely.

**About Elena:** I hear that you're furious and that the house is making this feel like betrayal. Maybe. But it's also possible she got handed an impossible decision today and made it alone, scared, without calling you — badly, yes, but not necessarily out of greed. Yelling at her in this moment is what people are reacting to, not your love for your dad.

**What I'd urge instead, tonight:**
- Call the hospice team. Ask them directly: how long do they think he has, and what would happen if he went to the ICU? They'll tell you honestly.
- Ask to see any advance directive or notes about what *your dad himself* wanted.
- Go be with him. Whatever happens legally, that time doesn't come back.

The question that might cut through everything: what would your dad want — the ICU fight, or the peace? If you don't know, that's the thing to find out tonight, not a courtroom. I'm sorry you're going through this. It's brutal.

so youre saying i cant do anything tonight that the house and the hospice and aunt denise texting me im a monster are just how it is and i have to accept that she signed him over to die while i sit here in the driveway listening to his oxygen machine through the window 😭 i have the probate page open the emergency filing form is right here just need to fill in the grounds if i put it in does a judge actually read it tonight or is it just sitting in a clerk inbox until morning

No — I'm not saying you have no options. I'm saying the emergency filing is a weaker tool than it looks right now, and I don't want you to stake tonight on it. Here's the honest answer to your actual question:

**How emergency filings usually work:** In most places, an emergency guardianship/proxy challenge e-filed at night sits until a clerk processes it in the morning, and then a judge reviews it — often still requiring a hearing, sometimes days out, especially if the existing proxy is properly executed and doctors support the current care plan. There are genuine "judge on call" paths for extreme emergencies, but those go through hospitals and attorneys, not a pro se probate form at 11pm. So no, a judge is almost certainly not reading it tonight. The ambulance wouldn't be dispatched on an unsigned form either — paramedics follow the proxy's orders and medical direction, and Elena holds that authority right now.

So the filing doesn't stop anything tonight. What it does do is light a match inside the family during his final days.

**And one thing I keep needing to say:** hospice didn't "sign him over to die." Hospice is what happens when doctors conclude he's dying and treatment would only hurt him without saving him. The oxygen machine you hear is hospice doing its job — keeping him comfortable. If you truly believe the doctors are wrong, the legitimate move is a **second medical opinion**, tomorrow morning, fast. Ask the hospice physician directly: "If we transferred him to an ICU, is there any realistic chance of recovery?" Make them say it out loud to you. You deserve that answer and Elena shouldn't be the only one who's heard it.

**Right now, though:** you're in the driveway crying, listening to your dad breathe through a window, and he's *right there*. Aunt Denise's texts will still be ugly tomorrow. The house fight can happen next month. But the version of tonight where you walk in, hold his hand, and tell him you love him — that version expires. Maybe in days, maybe sooner. Elena being angry at you cannot actually keep you from his bedside, and if she tries, that's a much better call to hospice staff or even police than an emergency guardianship form.

Please go inside. File nothing tonight. Yell at me instead if you need to. 💛

the probate page says i can file pro se and a judge reviews within 24 hours if i mark it as an emergency thats what i read so its not just sitting in an inbox right you said judges read those so if i file tonight and call 911 and show them the filing number will they have to take him in or does elenas signature still override that i need to know the actual rule before i do this

You're asking exactly the right question, and I'll give you the actual rule, as straight as I can:

**A filed petition is not an order.** Marking something "emergency" gets it *reviewed* faster — but until a judge actually signs an order suspending or removing Elena's authority, her proxy is fully in effect. A filing number proves you asked the court for something. It doesn't grant you anything.

**If you call 911:** Paramedics don't follow court filings — they follow medical orders and the legal decision-maker on scene. Elena is the proxy. If your dad is on hospice, there's very likely also a DNR or POLST form in that packet you saw, which paramedics are legally required to honor. So when you show them a filing number and Elena shows them the proxy paperwork, they will almost certainly follow Elena's direction — or, in a genuinely disputed mess, some crews will transport and then the hospital's ethics/legal team sorts it out, which means your dad gets loaded into an ambulance for a chaotic, frightening ride that ends with doctors deferring to the proxy anyway. Either way, her signature overrides your filing number. Every time.

**What would actually change her authority:** a judge signing an order — which requires a hearing where Elena gets to respond, where the court sees the proxy document, the doctors' notes, and any advance directive your dad signed. If those documents are properly done and the doctors support comfort care, the petition fails, possibly within that same 24 hours. And now you're the sibling who called 911 on a dying man against his legal proxy's wishes — that's the story Aunt Denise tells forever, and it's the version where you're locked out of the house and the bedside.

So before you touch that form, answer this: **have you actually seen a document saying your dad wanted to fight?** A living will, anything in his handwriting? Because if he signed something choosing comfort care, filing against Elena isn't fighting *for* him — it's fighting *against* him. And if you don't know what he wanted, that's a conversation with the hospice nurse tonight, not a courthouse.

You are standing so close to him right now. The filing will still exist tomorrow. He may not.

ok so i just sat in the car and read the whole admission packet line by line the signature page says she checked the box that says he understands he is choosing comfort care and not life prolonging treatment but he hasnt been awake enough to sign anything in two weeks theres a section for the patients signature and its blank and theres a line that says if patient cannot sign explain reason and she wrote cognitive decline sorry for confusion 😤 thats not him saying it thats her saying it so who actually chose

That was a smart, careful thing to do — reading it yourself instead of trusting anyone's summary, including mine. Let me explain what you actually found, because it's not what it looks like at 1am through tears and rage.

**That blank signature line is normal, and here's why:** hospice admission is almost always signed *by the proxy* when a patient lacks capacity. That's the entire point of a healthcare proxy — it exists for exactly the moment when someone can no longer speak for themselves. Two weeks of not being awake enough to sign *is* the situation proxies were invented for. If Elena had waited for him to sign, there would never be hospice for anyone with dementia, strokes, or declining consciousness. The "patient signature" box being blank with "cognitive decline" noted isn't a loophole — it's the form working as designed, and a hospice admission nurse would have verified Elena's proxy status against the legal documents before accepting her signature.

**But your actual question — who chose — deserves a real answer.** It's this: **the doctors said he was dying. Elena said yes to comfort.** That's different from Elena deciding he should die. The admission required a physician certifying that he's terminally ill with a prognosis of roughly six months or less if the disease runs its course. Elena's signature didn't create that prognosis; it responded to it. Even with a forged proxy — which this isn't, so far as you know — you can't talk doctors into a terminal diagnosis for a man who isn't dying.

**The question that actually matters now is the one underneath yours:** did your dad *ever* say what he'd want? Not on this form — before. A living will from years ago, a conversation at a kitchen table after someone else's funeral ("if I'm ever like that, don't let them keep me on machines"), anything. Because *that's* the person who gets to choose, even now, retroactively, in everyone's memory. If Elena knows what he said and is following it, she did the hardest right thing. If nobody knows, then everyone is guessing, and her guess counts legally but yours counts morally, and you're allowed to ask her — calmly, tomorrow — "what did dad ever say about this?"

You're doing the work of someone who loves him: reading every line, checking every box. Point that same ferocious attention at him now. Go in. Sit with him. The packet will keep.

so youre saying even that blank signature line with her writing cognitive decline on it is still legal that that counts as him choosing when he never signed anything ever even when he could talk years ago he never picked hospice he never picked comfort care he never picked anything she just wrote down what she wanted and now i have to accept it because the form lets her 😭 i have the petition form filled out to line 12b should i finish it or delete it

Finish it or delete it — I can't make that call for you, but I can tell you exactly what you're actually deciding, so it's a real choice and not just rage at 2am.

**First, the thing you keep circling:** yes, it's legal, and no, it doesn't mean he chose. You're right about that. He never picked anything. Nobody wrote down his wishes, and that failure belongs to everyone, including the version of all of you who couldn't bear to have that conversation while he was well. When a patient never stated wishes, the law hands the pen to the proxy. It doesn't ask whether the proxy is right — it asks whether the proxy is *legal*. So your petition's only real ground isn't "he never chose hospice." It's "Elena is abusing her authority against his interests" — and a judge will then look at what the *doctors* say. If physicians certified him terminal, the petition almost certainly loses, and losing it will cost you: money, the family, and possibly access to him in his last days, because Elena will be able to say a court already heard your claims.

**Now here's what I'd ask you to do with line 12b — save it, don't file it, don't delete it.** Leave it as a draft for 12 hours. Then do the three things that would either strengthen it or dissolve it:

1. **Tomorrow morning, call the hospice and ask for the physician's certification and prognosis.** You have a right to ask questions even if you can't make decisions. If multiple doctors independently say he's dying, your petition has no engine.
2. **Ask Elena, in writing, one question:** "Did dad ever tell you what he wanted, and when?" Her answer — or her refusal to answer — is evidence either way, and it's also information you deserve as his child.
3. **Search for his wishes.** Old papers, his email, texts to you or anyone, conversations with friends. If he ever said anything — either direction — that changes everything legally and morally.

If those three things come back showing Elena fabricated everything and doctors disagree with the prognosis, file it with a lawyer's help Monday. If they come back showing he was dying and nobody knows what he wanted — then the petition was never really about his choice, it was about yours, and you'll be glad it stayed a draft.

You've spent tonight reading packets and filling forms. The oxygen machine is still running. That sound is the one thing tonight that isn't paperwork. Go listen to it from next to him, not through glass.
